extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of 19th-century satirical prose / students of literary satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria for composing and interpreting satirical, political prose and letters—including interpretive rules for antique material, rhetorical strategies for ambiguous political speech, and cautions about stylistic compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of interpretation for antique cosmogonies and fables
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the common modern interpretive rule: find a common-sense meaning first, then select whatever can be imagined the most opposite thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated: 'to find a common-sense meaning, and then select whatever can be imagined the most opposite thereto.' The page recommends this method for antique cosmogonies, myths, fables, proverbial expressions, and knotty points generally—i.e., establish the plain sense and then deliberately imagine an opposite reading as an interpretive device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols and intentional ambiguity in political communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry ante-electionary dialogues by symbols or the language of signs so replies remain open to later retrospective construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit examples given: a candidate could 'convey a suitable reply to all committees of inquiry by closing one eye, or by presenting them with a phial of Egyptian darkness' or use undeciphered scripts (Dighton rock hieroglyphic, cuneiform) so every fresh decipherer 'educe[s] a different meaning.' Purpose: to enable the candidate to ‘take his position on either side of the fence with entire consistency.’ This is practical advice for hedging commitments in public/political writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware over-compression; brevity can expose superfluity
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed or extremely brief prose is still vulnerable: critics can detect and remove superfluous words even from the most concise styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the remark that 'There is scarce any style so compressed that superfluous words may not be detected in it.' Example: a severe critic might curtail Caesar's brevity by striking out the 'supererogatory veni and vidi.' Implication for writers: concision is not an automatic shield against critique; ensure each word carries necessary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and imitate classical exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant engagement with classical models is recommended as practice for writers and scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encapsulated in the Latin injunction 'Vos exemplaria Græca nocturna versate manu, versate diurna.' This suggests repeatedly turning Greek exemplars by day and night—i.e., persistent study and imitation of Greek literary models as a method of craft development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical/accounting method for critiquing valor and public reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mock-ledger or balance-sheet frameworks to juxtapose physical sacrifices/harms against public honors and rewards, revealing ironic mismatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by the mock account 'B. SAWIN, Esq., in account with (BLANK) GLORY' which lists credits (loss of limb, eye, ribs, service) versus debits (cheers, a suit of gray clothes, musical entertainments, chance of pension) summing each column to 100. Guidance: quantify and contrast costs and rewards to satirically evaluate the true value of 'glory' or public honors.
